deep.reconstruction:
This is a fair copy of the opening of Riemann's Inaugural Dissertation (Göttingen 1851), 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse', §1. The heading here reads 'Über Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The text agrees almost word for word with the printed version. There are no computations on the page, only definitions.

(a) Function concept (Dirichlet-style). Let z be a variable that can take, one after another, all real values. If to each value of z there corresponds a single value of the indeterminate quantity w, then w is called a function of z. In modern terms: a function is any single-valued assignment f: D ⊂ R → R, z ↦ w = f(z), with no requirement that it be given by a formula.

(b) Continuity on an interval. Suppose that while z runs continuously through all values between two fixed values a and b, w also changes continuously. Then f is called continuous ('stetig oder continuirlich') on [a,b]. Riemann gives no ε-δ formulation. In modern terms: for all z0 in [a,b], f(z) → f(z0) as z → z0.

(c) Remark. This definition imposes no law connecting the individual values of the function. If f is fixed on some interval, its continuation outside that interval is entirely arbitrary. Modern reading: real continuous functions have no identity theorem, so values on [a,b] do not determine f elsewhere.

Purpose: this remark sets up the contrast developed on the next page. By Weierstrass-type and Fourier-type representation results ('neuere Untersuchungen'), 'arbitrary continuous function' and 'given by an analytic expression' coincide for real variables. That equivalence breaks down when z = x + yi is complex. Riemann then imposes the condition that dw/dz be independent of the direction of dz (the Cauchy–Riemann equations). For complex-differentiable functions, continuation is no longer arbitrary: values on a piece determine the function (analytic continuation / identity theorem). The present page is only the real-variable preliminary.
errors: No mathematical errors. The continuity definition is informal ('stetig durchläuft … stetig sich ändert'), which is standard for 1851 and not an error.
The claim that a function's continuation outside an interval is wholly arbitrary is correct for real continuous functions.

results.what: General (arbitrary-correspondence) definition of a real function of a real variable
Definition of continuity of a function on an interval
results.modern_name: Continuity on an interval (pre-ε-δ, Cauchy/Bolzano style)

results.what: Observation that the values of a real function on an interval impose no law on its extension outside it (contrast later drawn with complex-differentiable functions)
results.modern_name: Absence of an identity theorem / rigidity for real continuous functions (motivating analytic continuation)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a near-verbatim manuscript (fair copy) of §1 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation. The content is well known and routinely attributed to him. The only historical interest is the title variant 'Über Functionen …' and that this is a draft or fair copy of the dissertation.

checkable.asserts: Two functions continuous on [0,1] that agree there can differ outside it: real continuation is arbitrary.

checkable.sympy: limit(Piecewise((x**2, x<=1), (2*x-1, True)), x, 1, '+') == limit(Piecewise((x**2, x<=1), (2*x-1, True)), x, 1, '-')
checkable.asserts: An arbitrary extension (here 2x-1) can even be chosen to keep continuity at the boundary, illustrating the non-uniqueness of continuation.
